subtitle: Useful knowledge and skills matter, and so does openness. This course helps you build both while staying receptive to another person’s meaning, their corrections and their real choices.
scope: For staff across DHS. Cultural humility and cultural competence are compared through direct conceptual sources and original learning examples. The course does not claim that all competence models are static or that humility replaces practical skill. Personal reflection can remain private and unrecorded; the practice path is complete. No IDI assessment or individual orientation is inferred. Actual agency decisions and required processes remain in place. Native American- and Tribal-specific matters are referred to the person or area responsible within ADSA.
introTranscript: Knowledge matters. So does the ability to recognize when your knowledge does not answer another person’s experience. This course explores that relationship through Rowan and Sage, who disagree about what it means to preserve a meaningful object. A separate DHS orientation example connects knowledge, listening and practical capacity. You can learn through an example or reflect privately without submitting a personal story or proving a workplace result.

intro.heading: Compare the approaches without creating rivals
intro.body:
Tervalon and Murray-García’s 1998 medical-education paper challenges a view of competence as finished mastery and proposes ongoing self-examination, attention to power and partnership. Its clinical discussion is historical. It does not establish that every later competence model treats culture as a fixed body of facts.

The National Center for Cultural Competence describes its framework as developmental and includes self-assessment and adaptation as well as knowledge. The approaches therefore need not be presented as “competence knows everything; humility knows nothing.” Such a comparison would distort the sources and give learners a false choice.

In this example, Rowan studies the history of a meaningful household object inherited by friend Sage. Rowan learns the object’s likely period, materials and common use. That knowledge can be useful. Rowan then assumes Sage must value the object as an untouched display piece. Sage volunteers a different meaning: using it carefully in daily life keeps a relationship with a loved person present.

Knowledge of history and openness to Sage’s meaning answer different questions. Rowan need not abandon the research. Rowan does need to stop treating the research as an answer to what the object should mean for Sage. Learning both can develop understanding without ranking either friend or requiring a real household example.

flashcards.back: Developing the knowledge, skills and organizational capacities needed to work effectively across cultural contexts; definitions differ among models.
Ongoing self-examination, attention to unequal influence and respectful learning with others.
Treating useful knowledge as complete knowledge of a person or situation.
What an object, practice or interaction has come to signify through a person’s experience and affiliations.
The actual resources, skills and arrangements needed to respond, beyond an expression of good intention.
New information that can change an interpretation or a response without making the learner’s whole background wrong.

items.title: A useful distinction
items.body: Historical information concerns what the object was made for and how it has been used. Sage’s account concerns what this particular object means now. Confusing those questions turns knowledge into ownership of someone else’s interpretation. Keeping them distinct lets the research and the relationship each contribute something relevant.

items.title: Avoid a false opposition
items.body: Competence can include continued learning and organizational change. Humility can involve informed, skillful action. Describing one as certainty and the other as ignorance makes it harder to see what each asks of the learner. Compare the actual model or practice rather than rely on the connotations of the label.

items.title: Do not turn labels into a ranking
items.body: Calling Rowan competent or humble does not show what Rowan understood or did. A specific account is more useful: Rowan learned the object’s history and reconsidered an unsupported assumption about Sage. That description leaves room for another question rather than assigning a permanent status.

tabs.label: Knowledge as ownership
tabs.body: Rowan uses the research to decide what Sage ought to value. The knowledge may be accurate, but it is being used to answer a different question. This can make Sage’s account appear like an error rather than relevant information about a personal meaning.

tabs.label: Openness without learning
tabs.body: Rowan refuses to learn anything about the object because only Sage’s meaning matters. This preserves one perspective by discarding another useful question. The history may help Rowan understand the object and ask a better question without replacing Sage’s account.

tabs.label: Knowledge with inquiry
tabs.body: Rowan shares the historical information as one contribution and listens to Sage’s present meaning. This allows understanding to grow in two directions. Neither the research nor the personal account has to become the only legitimate source for every question.

check.question: Which comparison is supported by these sources?
check.correct: Humility emphasizes ongoing reflection and relationships; competence models can also include development, self-assessment and adaptation.
wrong: All competence models teach that cultural learning is finished.
Humility means useful knowledge and skill should be abandoned.
The two terms provide a reliable ranking of people.
check.feedbackCorrect: The comparison distinguishes emphases without misrepresenting all competence models or discarding practical knowledge. The actual model and situation matter.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The NCCC framework is developmental, so a universal fixed-endpoint claim is false. Humility does not require ignorance, and labels do not rank people’s actual practice. Compare the specific knowledge, openness and capacity demonstrated in the situation.

items.text: Rowan researched the object’s likely period.
Sage associates daily use with remembering a loved person.
Historical research decides what Sage must value.
Rowan learned about the material.
Sage says the object feels present in everyday life.
Every competence model claims complete mastery.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: Rowan, a DHS staff member, uses the practice object example for private learning. Rowan has accurate historical information but assumed it reveals what Sage must value.
scenario.prompt: Which next response combines knowledge and humility?
options: Insist the research gives Rowan the final say.

responses: Accurate history does not give ownership of another person’s meaning.

lessons.transfer: Use the practice object or privately consider a meaningful practice. Separate knowledge about it from what it means to you; no account needs to be entered.

move.control: You can distinguish the questions answered by knowledge and by a person’s account.
move.failure: The comparison becomes a choice between complete mastery and complete ignorance.
move.next: Name a useful piece of knowledge and a meaning it does not settle.

lessons.statement: Ask a better question rather than turn context into a prediction.

image.caption: Colleagues share information and consider a decision together.

intro.heading: Let knowledge improve the question
intro.body:
Rowan’s research says objects of this kind were sometimes saved for special occasions. Rowan is tempted to ask Sage why they are not following the “proper” custom. That question already treats one historical pattern as a rule and Sage’s choice as a deviation.

A different question could be, “What matters to you about keeping it in everyday use?” Sage may explain the remembered relationship, choose not to discuss it or say that the use is simply convenient. Each possibility needs room. The question should not demand proof of an authentic tradition.

Contextual knowledge can reveal possibilities you had not considered. It cannot make one person’s affiliations, family practices or intentions predictable. Even a careful account has a time, place and purpose. The source may describe a pattern without describing Sage’s experience.

Rowan can also learn something personal: preservation originally meant protecting an object from wear. Sage’s account introduces another meaning of preservation—maintaining a connection through use. Understanding that difference is worthwhile even if Rowan does not change a real habit. It need not be converted into a workplace metric.

inThisLesson: Use contextual information without assigning a script to a person.
Distinguish a historical account from an individual’s present meaning.
Develop a relevant question that allows correction.
What should Rowan avoid?
lessons.keyStatement: Ask a better question rather than turn context into a prediction.

items.title: Watch the premise in the question
items.body: “Why do you break the custom?” asks Sage to defend against a claim that has not been established. “What matters about this use?” asks for a relevant meaning without assuming it. The wording matters because a question can impose an interpretation as easily as a statement.

items.title: Keep source scope visible
items.body: A historical pattern can be accurate within the source and still not predict Sage’s present practice. Rowan can say what was learned and where it applies. A limited source is not useless; its value improves when it is used for the question it actually addresses.

items.title: Allow a different answer
items.body: Sage may not want to discuss the relationship or may value the object for another reason. The inquiry remains useful if Rowan accepts that choice. A demand for a preferred story would make the person’s participation serve Rowan’s learning rather than their own discretion.

tabs.label: Test authenticity
tabs.body: Rowan asks whether Sage is following the tradition correctly. This makes Sage’s personal use answerable to Rowan’s reading. It can imply that deviation from a described pattern is cultural failure, even though the source has not supplied a rule for this person.

tabs.label: Ask without context
tabs.body: Rowan asks vaguely what culture means to Sage. The invitation is broad and may ask for more personal explanation than the situation needs. A specific question about the object offers a clearer purpose and makes it easier to decide whether to answer.

tabs.label: Ask about the relevant meaning
tabs.body: Rowan explains the historical interest and asks what matters about daily use. The question keeps context useful while allowing Sage’s account or a decision not to share. It can reveal a perspective difference without demanding a whole personal history.

check.question: Which question best uses the research without imposing it?
check.correct: What matters to you about keeping this object in everyday use?
wrong: Why are you failing to follow the proper custom?
Which group identity explains your choice?
How can you prove your practice is authentic?
check.feedbackCorrect: The question concerns the actual use and permits Sage to describe its meaning or decline. It does not turn context into an authenticity test.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A failure premise invents a rule, group identity does not determine this choice, and authenticity proof makes personal meaning answerable to a test. Use a relevant question that leaves the person’s actual answer open.

items.text: The source describes some special-occasion uses.
What matters about everyday use for you?
Prove your practice is authentic.
The source concerns a particular time and setting.
Would you like to discuss this, or leave it private?
Your use must match my source to be valid.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: Rowan has read about special-occasion uses of the object. Sage’s everyday use differs from that pattern.
options: Treating the historical pattern as a test of Sage’s authenticity.
Keeping the source’s time and setting clear.
Offering a relevant question with room to decline.
responses: That turns contextual information into an unestablished personal rule.
Keeping scope clear improves the use of knowledge; it is appropriate.
A relevant optional question preserves the person’s choice; it is appropriate.

lessons.transfer: Privately compare a source about a practice with one meaning it might not settle. Fiction is enough, and no personal explanation is required.

move.control: You can make the question specific and its premise open.
move.failure: Context becomes an authenticity test or a prediction from identity.
move.next: Ask about a relevant meaning and accept that the person may choose not to explain it.

lessons.statement: Be open about limits while developing the skills the task needs.

intro.heading: Develop skills without claiming complete understanding
intro.body:
Rowan wants to photograph the object for Sage. Rowan learns how to light the surface without reflections and produces an image that shows the detail Sage requested. This is a practical skill applied to a specific task. It does not establish complete understanding of why the object matters.

The two questions can coexist: can Rowan make the requested image, and does Rowan understand the meaning Sage volunteered? Skill does not replace listening, while respectful listening does not create photographic ability. Humility can support preparation because it makes a gap easier to recognize rather than conceal.

Suppose Rowan has not learned how to handle fragile material safely. An honest response is to state that limit and explore an appropriate resource or a different plan with Sage. Rowan should not experiment merely to prove willingness. Nor should Rowan call the task impossible simply because one skill is missing.

For DHS work, the same distinction can apply to accurate information, accessible communication or a service procedure. Those tasks have actual requirements and roles. Saying “I am humble and still learning” cannot authorize unqualified interpretation or substitute for required preparation. This conceptual lesson does not set a technical qualification; it asks learners to recognize when the task needs one.

lessons.keyStatement: Be open about limits while developing the skills the task needs.

items.title: Specify the skill
items.body: Rowan can produce the requested image under the conditions practiced. That is a clearer claim than “Rowan understands this culture.” A specific skill can be developed, used and checked without making it evidence of complete interpersonal understanding or permanent mastery.

items.title: A limit can prevent avoidable harm
items.body: Fragility creates a handling question that enthusiasm does not answer. Rowan can pause and ask about suitable support before acting. Naming the limit is not a confession of failure; it makes a responsible next choice possible and avoids making Sage pay for an improvised demonstration.

items.title: Keep the person in the choice
items.body: Sage can choose whether a different image or support would be useful. Rowan should explain the relevant skill gap without turning Sage into an instructor obliged to solve it. Seeking another resource can retain both respect for Sage’s choice and responsibility for Rowan’s own learning.

tabs.label: Confidence without capacity
tabs.body: Rowan says willingness is enough and handles the fragile object without preparation. This treats openness as a substitute for skill. The risk comes from an unanswered task question, not from a lack of polite words, and Sage’s permission to discuss meaning does not answer handling safety.

tabs.label: Capacity without inquiry
tabs.body: Rowan produces a technically excellent image but ignores which feature Sage wanted captured. The skill is real, yet its use may miss the purpose. A suitable result requires understanding the relevant request as well as executing the technique.

tabs.label: Preparation with openness
tabs.body: Rowan clarifies the feature, names the handling limit and seeks suitable support before making a promise. This joins a real skill with a real purpose. If a different plan is needed, the person can consider it without receiving false assurance.

check.question: What does a successful requested photograph establish?
check.correct: A specific task was completed; it does not prove complete cultural understanding or every related skill.
wrong: Rowan now understands every meaning of the object.
Humility removes the need to prepare for handling fragile materials.
The skill gives Rowan authority to override Sage’s purpose.
check.feedbackCorrect: The achievement concerns the requested task. Its scope remains useful and specific rather than expanding into mastery of the person or permission for unprepared action.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A photograph cannot reveal every personal meaning. Humility does not remove preparation, and technical skill does not own the task’s purpose. Keep skill, understanding and authority distinct so each unanswered question can be addressed.

items.text: Rowan can photograph the requested surface detail.
Safe handling of the fragile object has not been established.
The image proves complete cultural understanding.
Rowan knows how to avoid reflections in this setup.
A suitable handling resource is still needed.
Good intention replaces every qualification.

scenario.prompt: Which next choice joins skill and humility?
options: Explain the handling limit and explore suitable support or a different plan.
Declare all existing photographic skill useless.
responses: Willingness does not answer the safety question.
This preserves the real skill and identifies the gap before making a promise or acting.
A relevant gap does not erase useful knowledge; it points to the next need.

lessons.transfer: Use the practice skill or privately identify one capability and one remaining question. No public account or proof of improvement is needed.

move.control: You can make a specific capability claim and name the gap honestly.
move.failure: Good intention becomes an excuse for unprepared action, or one gap erases all useful skill.
move.next: Identify what you can do, what the task still needs and a suitable resource.

intro.heading: Connect personal reflection with practical response
intro.body:
Rowan reflects privately on why an untouched object seemed the best form of preservation. In the practice account, carefully stored belongings represented responsible care. Rowan feared that use would erase a remembered person. This explains the reaction without making it the only legitimate meaning.

Sage’s account suggests another possibility: use can sustain a relationship by bringing memory into daily life. Rowan need not decide that storage is wrong. Rowan can understand that two meanings of care lead to different choices, then ask which purpose matters to Sage in this situation.

The reflection itself can broaden Rowan’s personal understanding. A later action might be offering the requested photograph without urging Sage to display the object unused. That action gives the clarified meaning a place in the response, but its effect is not known merely because Rowan intended it well.

This is not a test of who is more humble or competent. It is a way to see how knowledge, self-examination and a behavioral choice can connect. A practice or silent reflection path is enough; sharing a memory, documenting a change or producing a workplace outcome is not needed.

Use new meaning to reconsider a response without abandoning an honest value.
Distinguish private insight from a claim that an interaction improved.
What can Rowan accurately say?
lessons.keyStatement: Let reflection inform a response without making either insight or effect automatic.

items.title: Keep a value and question its reach
items.body: Responsible care matters to Rowan. The unsupported extension was assuming storage is always the best expression of it. Examining that extension can preserve the value while making another person’s purpose intelligible. It avoids replacing a rigid rule with the equally rigid instruction to reject one’s own background.

items.title: An alternative meaning changes the choice
items.body: Once Rowan recognizes daily use as remembrance, urging permanent storage may no longer fit Sage’s purpose. The changed response has a cultural reason rather than being generic politeness. Rowan can still mention a practical handling concern without treating that concern as authority over the object’s personal meaning.

items.title: Insight and effect are separate
items.body: Rowan can honestly say the preservation assumption changed. That does not establish that Sage felt understood or that the relationship improved. The distinction allows personal learning to count while preventing it from being used as evidence for an unexamined interpersonal outcome.

tabs.label: Reject the old value
tabs.body: Rowan concludes that careful storage was a foolish learned practice. This treats perspective-taking as a demand to disown a meaningful background. The better question is whether that practice should decide Sage’s purpose, not whether it can ever be worthwhile.

tabs.label: Retain the old conclusion
tabs.body: Rowan understands Sage’s account but still insists the object must be displayed unused. New information is heard without affecting the choice. The reason for the insistence should be examined rather than hidden behind a claim of listening.

tabs.label: Broaden the understanding
tabs.body: Rowan keeps the value of responsible care and recognizes another expression of remembrance. The response can now fit Sage’s purpose more closely without false agreement or a universal rule. Personal insight may remain private even if the choice later changes.

check.question: What is a valid outcome of Rowan’s private reflection?
check.correct: A broader understanding of preservation and care, even if no work product or shared story follows.
wrong: Proof that Sage feels fully understood.
A requirement to reject Rowan’s own learned value.
A completed ranking of both friends’ cultural development.
check.feedbackCorrect: Personal understanding is a meaningful result on its own. It does not certify another person’s response, require self-rejection or assess either friend.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Private insight cannot prove Sage’s feelings. Perspective-taking does not require rejecting a learned value, and the exercise cannot rank development. Name the actual understanding gained without turning it into a stronger claim.

items.text: Storage is one meaningful way Rowan learned care.
Rowan offers the requested photograph without imposing a display rule.
Sage’s later reaction is not yet known.
Daily use can carry a different meaning of remembrance.
Rowan asks which purpose Sage wants the image to serve.
No information establishes that the relationship improved.

lessons.transfer: Choose the practice meanings or a private value of your own. You can stop with understanding and leave any further action optional.

move.control: You can connect a clarified meaning with a choice while keeping effect claims accurate.
move.failure: Insight is discounted without a work receipt or inflated into proof of another person’s response.
move.next: State the understanding gained and, if useful, a response it might inform.

lessons.statement: Connect listening with an actual capacity and responsible next step.

intro.heading: Give openness the capacity to matter at work
intro.body:
In a separate practice DHS orientation exercise, coordinator Alex says newcomers can ask questions freely. Participant Jamie explains a learned meaning of respect: raising an unfinished question publicly can feel like challenging the facilitator before understanding their purpose. Jamie would welcome an opportunity to think first and choose whether to ask in the group.

Alex originally saw immediate public questions as evidence of engagement. Jamie’s account changes the interpretation. The issue is not automatically a language need, disability or a rule for Jamie’s whole community. It is a volunteered meaning in this particular learning situation.

Alex can consider feasible ways to make questions available before discussion and explain the purpose of the activity. But an offer needs the actual time, information and contribution route to work. A promise of a private follow-up that nobody can provide is not practical capacity. Alex should distinguish what is available from what requires an authorized change.

A relevant adjustment may support this orientation activity without changing required training, actual criteria or any participant’s formal request. The authorized employment accommodation process remains separate. If a protected-class allegation arises, a manager’s immediate HR or agency Affirmative Action Officer reporting under MMB Policy 1436 cannot wait for an informal discussion. The DHS Equity Policy’s required analysis also remains applicable to the actual work; this practice preparation does not replace it.

Identify how a contribution can inform a relevant orientation choice.
Preserve actual work, accommodation and reporting responsibilities.
Which response fits the actual role?
lessons.keyStatement: Connect listening with an actual capacity and responsible next step.

items.title: A volunteered meaning changes the reading
items.body: Jamie’s hesitation does not necessarily mean lack of interest. Alex learns that timing can carry a meaning of respectful preparation. The response can acknowledge that meaning without deciding Jamie’s identity, proficiency or orientation and without requiring a personal history to justify the contribution.

items.title: An available route matters
items.body: If questions are offered beforehand, participants need to receive them in time and know how to contribute. The promise and the usable route are separate. Checking the actual arrangement makes listening more than a pleasant invitation while avoiding claims that one method resolves everyone’s need.

items.title: Responsibility does not move to the contributor
items.body: Jamie need not design all orientation or represent every newcomer. Alex remains responsible for the assigned work and can seek consultant guidance as useful. The proper owners decide any changes outside Alex’s authority; a participant’s meaningful account does not bypass those roles.

tabs.label: Welcome alone
tabs.body: Alex repeats that all questions are welcome but leaves immediate public participation as the only option. The statement is positive, yet the clarified meaning has no relevant place to affect the activity. It should not be reported as a change in capacity merely because it sounds inclusive.

tabs.label: Promise without a route
tabs.body: Alex offers a private conversation to every newcomer without checking availability. The offer may create expectations the program cannot meet. Honest limits and a feasible alternative are more useful than calling an unsupported promise humble or competent.

tabs.label: Clarify and prepare
tabs.body: Alex explains the activity’s purpose, identifies feasible advance questions and states what requires further review. This connects the cultural meaning to a practical choice within actual responsibility. The result still needs appropriate task feedback before claiming participation improved.

check.question: What combines cultural learning and practical capacity in this case?
check.correct: Use Jamie’s volunteered meaning to examine a feasible participation route, while keeping actual authority and required processes intact.
wrong: Treat Jamie as a spokesperson for every newcomer.
Promise any desired option without checking resources.
Use welcoming language as proof the participation route works.
check.feedbackCorrect: The response connects a specific meaning to a real choice. It remains honest about resources, roles and what needs further review.
check.feedbackIncorrect: One account does not represent every newcomer. Unchecked promises can fail, and welcome alone does not establish usability. Consider the actual route and responsible roles instead of inflating input, intention or assurance into a completed result.

items.text: Jamie links thinking before a question with respect.
Alex checks whether advance questions can actually be supplied.
Jamie represents all newcomers.
Immediate questioning means engagement to Alex.
A manager immediately reports a protected-class allegation under Policy 1436.
A welcoming invitation proves everyone can participate.

intro.heading: Continue learning with accurate claims
intro.body:
Rowan can describe several results: new historical knowledge, a practiced photographic skill and a broader understanding of preservation. These are useful but different. None establishes complete knowledge of Sage or everyone who values a similar object.

Alex can describe a prepared orientation arrangement and the meaning that informed it. Whether newcomers can use the route is a further task question. A thank-you may show appreciation, while missing feedback leaves an effect unknown. Neither should become a claim that all barriers disappeared.

An ongoing approach to competence can identify the next skill or resource. Humility can keep that learning responsive to correction and to whose meaning or voice is missing. Their relationship is practical rather than a competition for the better label.

A next step should fit the path. Rowan may continue private reflection without producing anything. Alex may review a relevant participation task through authorized methods, protect personal information and use required equity-analysis procedures when applicable. There is no universal requirement in this exercise to gather sensitive data or compare every group. Appropriate evidence depends on the actual question and responsibilities.

inThisLesson: Distinguish knowledge, practiced skill, reflection and observed results.
Identify a useful next learning step without claiming complete mastery.
Describe missing evidence honestly while valuing private understanding.
What can each accurately say?
lessons.keyStatement: Say what you learned or did, and leave unexamined effects open.

items.title: A specific progress statement helps
items.body: “I learned about the object’s materials” and “I reconsidered what preservation means” show different kinds of learning. Specific claims make another question easier to identify. “I am now culturally competent” gives far less information and may encourage treating further correction as unnecessary.

items.title: A task result needs task evidence
items.body: Providing questions is a concrete action. Whether the contribution route was usable requires relevant information about that activity. Alex can check a suitable question through the actual process rather than gather private stories or make a universal claim from one response.

items.title: A private path can remain complete
items.body: Rowan can value a changed understanding without seeking another person’s approval or creating a work receipt. Personal insight does not establish a professional outcome, but it does not need to. Keeping the paths distinct supports meaningful whole-person learning and accurate workplace reporting.

tabs.label: Completion as mastery
tabs.body: The course is complete, so a learner declares that future cultural questions are settled. This confuses participation with lasting knowledge of people and contexts. Completion can support continued learning; it cannot make new information irrelevant or assign a personal orientation.

tabs.label: Only measurable work counts
tabs.body: The learner dismisses private understanding because it has no workplace metric. That narrows learning unnecessarily and may encourage collecting personal information simply to demonstrate progress. Insight can be worthwhile while actual professional effect claims remain evidence-based.

tabs.label: Progress with an open next question
tabs.body: The learner names the knowledge, skill or insight gained and identifies any relevant remaining question. This makes progress visible without a claim of final mastery. The next step can be private learning, useful preparation or a responsible work review depending on the path.

check.question: Which final statement is most accurate?
check.correct: Useful knowledge, skill and private insight can each be named; any professional effect needs relevant evidence and no claim of complete mastery.
wrong: Course completion settles every later cultural question.
No feedback proves the orientation route works for everyone.
Private reflection only counts when documented for a supervisor.
check.feedbackCorrect: The statement distinguishes kinds of learning from outcome evidence. It supports continued development and private understanding without overclaiming professional results.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Completion does not settle new questions. Missing feedback does not prove universal success, and private reflection need not be reported to count. Use a specific claim that fits the knowledge or result actually available.

items.text: Rowan understands a new meaning of preservation.
Alex has supplied advance orientation questions.
An appropriate review shows a participant used the contribution route for this activity.
Completion establishes knowledge of everyone’s culture.
A relevant task check documents which question remained unresolved.
No feedback proves universal access.

lessons.next: Use the job aid to keep knowledge, skill, openness and actual responsibilities connected.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: Alex supplied the orientation questions but has not yet received relevant feedback about use. Rowan gained a private insight and has not shared it.
options: Both have proved every cultural barrier is gone.
Alex prepared a route whose effect is still unknown; Rowan’s private insight is a meaningful learning result.
Neither has made any useful progress.
responses: That overstates the information and scope.
This distinguishes preparation, unknown effect and intrinsic personal understanding.
Preparation and insight can be useful even when a separate effect is not yet established.

lessons.transfer: Privately name your learning through the practice or personal path. If applying it at work, keep outcome claims limited to relevant authorized evidence.

move.control: You can distinguish learning, preparation and actual effect.
move.failure: A label, completion or missing feedback becomes proof of mastery or universal benefit.
move.next: State the result you actually have and a useful next question if needed.

jobAid.subtitle: Compare the approaches through useful questions rather than a ranking of people.
remember: Competence models can be developmental; humility does not require abandoning knowledge or skill.
Context informs inquiry without deciding another person’s meaning.
Private insight is worthwhile without a submitted story or work result.
Actual professional effects and decisions need their appropriate evidence and authority.

sections.heading: Use what you know
items: What question does this knowledge actually answer?
What meaning, skill or task question remains open?
Am I treating a pattern as a rule for a person?

sections.heading: Stay open and prepare
items: What learned value informs my interpretation?
Can a volunteered meaning change my response without demanding disclosure?
What skill or practical resource does the task still need?
Which limits and choices can I explain honestly?

sections.heading: Follow through accurately
items: Keep staff responsibility and authorized decisions with their actual roles.
Use required equity-analysis, accommodation and reporting processes when applicable.
Separate personal insight, prepared action and observed effect.
Choose a private, practice or work next step that fits the actual question.

sources.title: Tervalon and Murray-García: Cultural humility versus cultural competence
sources.note: Historical primary medical-education argument about finished mastery, ongoing reflection, power and partnership. The course does not generalize this critique to every competence model or reproduce clinical cases, statistics or historical mandates.

sources.title: National Center for Cultural Competence: Frameworks and guiding principles
sources.note: The center’s own developmental framework includes self-assessment, cultural knowledge and adaptation. This conceptual source is not imported as a new DHS delegation, service rule or assessment exercise.

sources.title: National Center for Cultural Competence: Self-assessment
sources.note: Direct statement that cultural and linguistic competence develop over time. No source checklist, scoring tool or proprietary item is reproduced.

sources.title: DHS Equity Policy
sources.note: Actual equity-analysis and learning expectations remain applicable to DHS work. Course learning does not replace required training or authorized decisions.

sources.title: MMB Policy 1436: Harassment and discrimination prohibited
sources.note: The immediate manager and supervisor reporting duty and assigned agency procedures stay separate from learning and informal conversation.
